title: Fast and accurate neural triage decoding of ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes
authors: Hong-Ye Hu, Zhenlai Wang, Binzhao Luo, Tao Xiang, Chen Zhao
abstract: Quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing. High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have emerged as a promising approach to reducing the substantial physical qubit overhead of quantum error correction, enabling encoding rates exceeding $1/2$ in blocks of approximately one thousand physical data qubits. However, their practical implementation requires decoders that combine high accuracy with low latency to keep pace with quantum hardware. Existing decoders of high-rate qLDPC codes can achieve high accuracy but often incur substantial computational latency, whereas neural network decoders have yet to be demonstrated for high-rate qLDPC codes. Here, we introduce \emph{neural triage decoding}, a framework that uses syndrome consistency to adaptively allocate neural computation. A local neural message-passing network rapidly predicts error corrections, additional iterations reduce residual syndrome violations, and a rarely invoked diversification stage searches for consistent corrections to the remaining shots. We demonstrate that the \texttt{Triage} decoder can decode ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes encoding a few hundred logical qubits, including lifted-product and Kasai codes, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy comparable to the near optimal algorithmic decoders while reducing decoding latency by approximately one to two orders of magnitude. Our framework is inspired by a rigorous analysis of the exact bitwise marginal decoder, revealing a distance-independent syndrome-inconsistent error floor. In addition, we show the robustness of neural network decoders to mismatched error priors. Our results establish adaptive neural decoding as a promising route towards fast, accurate, and scalable quantum error correction in the near term.

infographic.key_insight: Neural triage decoding adaptively allocates computation to achieve high accuracy and low latency for ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce decoding bottlenecks in low-overhead quantum error correction by reserving expensive computation for difficult error patterns.
method: Use a local neural message-passing network to rapidly predict error corrections.
Apply additional iterations when residual syndrome violations remain.
Rarely invoke a diversification stage to search for syndrome-consistent corrections.
infographic.evidence_signal: On lifted-product and Kasai codes encoding hundreds of logical qubits, the abstract reports accuracy comparable to near-optimal algorithmic decoders with approximately 10–100× lower decoding latency.
infographic.watch_item: Real-time deployment requires checking worst-case latency from difficult shots and ensuring syndrome-consistent corrections do not introduce logical errors.
infographic.paper_title: Fast and accurate neural triage decoding of ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes

title: Symmetry-Preserving Hierarchical Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm with Subproblems Beyond the Qubit Limit
authors: Zhaoyang Song, Wei Zhang, Ji Cao, Xuexi Yi, Hong-Fu Wang
abstract: The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is a paradigmatic variational quantum algorithm for combinatorial optimization problems, yet on current quantum devices the available qubit count and achievable circuit depth remain the main bottlenecks to its practical application. Divide-and-merge reduces the number of variables encoded in a single quantum circuit, while contraction based on coarse graining extends the effective range of shallow circuits, but existing work has not addressed both challenges simultaneously. We propose symmetry-preserving hierarchical QAOA (SP-HQAOA), in which parity sector contraction preserves the zero-field Ising structure of the effective objective at every contraction step, thereby addressing both within a single algorithm. We further prove that this reduction is the unique one with this property. Successive contractions further decouple the maximum leaf block size $B$ from the qubit limit $Q$ per quantum call, so every quantum circuit uses at most $Q$ qubits even when $B>Q$. We also establish a deterministic repair-risk bound on the possible loss in optimal value caused by each sector restriction, and the resulting bounds can be summed across contraction steps and levels of the recursive hierarchy. With depth $p=1$, SP-HQAOA attains $99.4\%$ to $99.7\%$ of the exact optimum on $N=40$ random regular MaxCut leaf blocks and, with at most $10$ qubits per circuit, $96\%$ of the classical reference for $N=500$. SP-HQAOA demonstrates the capacity to use shallow quantum circuits to address combinatorial optimization problems whose variable count far exceeds the qubit limit of a single quantum call, and may enable practical quantum optimization advantages in the near term.

infographic.key_insight: SP-HQAOA combines hierarchical decomposition with symmetry-preserving contraction to optimize problems larger than a quantum device’s qubit limit using shallow circuits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Leaf subproblems can exceed the per-call qubit budget while every quantum circuit remains within that budget.
method: Recursively divide and merge optimization subproblems.
Contract parity sectors while preserving the zero-field Ising objective structure.
Bound potential optimal-value loss from sector restrictions and sum bounds across the hierarchy.
infographic.evidence_signal: At depth p=1, the abstract reports 99.4–99.7% of the exact optimum on N=40 random regular MaxCut leaf blocks and 96% of a classical reference for N=500 using at most 10 qubits per circuit.
infographic.watch_item: Sector restrictions can sacrifice solution quality; these benchmarks alone do not establish practical quantum advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Symmetry-Preserving Hierarchical Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm with Subproblems Beyond the Qubit Limit

title: Adiabatic training of VQAs for entanglement detection
authors: E. Acosta, C. Cano, D. Manzano, G. Botella
abstract: This paper introduces a hybrid quantum framework for training Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) aimed at addressing the fundamental problem of entanglement detection using adiabatic quantum computing. This problem is of foundational significance in quantum information science and has been approached through both classical and quantum methodologies. We propose an adiabatic-inspired optimization strategy for training VQAs, which combines a discretization of the parameter space with a hierarchical segmentation scheme. The optimization problem is formulated as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model to leverage the capabilities of quantum annealing. Preliminary results are compared against classical neural networks and conventional VQA training techniques. The findings aim to stimulate further investigation and discussion within the scientific community regarding the efficacy and applicability of the proposed approach.

infographic.key_insight: An adiabatic-inspired approach recasts VQA training for entanglement detection as a QUBO problem suitable for quantum annealing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers an alternative optimization route for hybrid quantum workflows, though practical performance advantages remain unestablished.
method: Discretize the VQA parameter space.
Apply a hierarchical segmentation scheme.
Formulate training as a QUBO to leverage quantum annealing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports preliminary comparisons with classical neural networks and conventional VQA training, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Parameter discretization may introduce accuracy–resource trade-offs that require validation at larger scales.
infographic.paper_title: Adiabatic training of VQAs for entanglement detection

title: Digital-Analog Quantum Neural Network with Long-Range Interactions
authors: Zongyuan Ge, Daili Li, Zewen Zhang
abstract: Protocols combining single-qubit digital operations with analog quantum evolutions bypass large numbers of two-qubit entangling gates, offering a promising approach to variational algorithms and hybrid quantum simulation. Focusing on the digital-analog quantum neural network (DA-QNN) as a representative framework, this work demonstrates that incorporating long-range interactions enhances the efficiency of such hybrid algorithms. Within the analog blocks, an Ising model with power-law interactions is employed to generate entanglement, and this protocol is benchmarked across supervised and unsupervised learning tasks. Beyond discussing the effects of the transverse field and evolution time, the primary analysis focuses on how the interaction range governs the expressibility and trainability of the ansatz. For supervised image classification and many-body phase detection, long-range ansatzes match the performance of their short-range counterparts with fewer DA-QNN layers or shorter evolution times, owing to the rapid information propagation across the system enabled by nonlocal couplings. This resource reduction alleviates the classical optimization overhead and eases experimental implementation. In unsupervised phase detection, although the long-range ansatz does not outperform its short-range counterpart in every regime, the two ansatzes provide complementary signatures that jointly reconstruct the complete phase diagram. These findings establish long-range interacting platforms as a compelling resource for advancing practical, large-scale digital-analog quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: Long-range interactions let digital-analog quantum neural networks match short-range performance on supervised tasks with fewer layers or shorter evolution times.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining single-qubit gates with long-range analog entanglement can reduce circuit resources and classical optimization overhead, potentially easing implementation.
method: Alternate digital single-qubit operations with analog Ising evolution using power-law interactions.
Study how interaction range, transverse field, and evolution time affect expressibility and trainability.
Benchmark supervised image classification and many-body phase detection, plus unsupervised phase detection.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports reduced layer or evolution-time requirements for supervised benchmarks and complementary long- and short-range signatures in unsupervised phase detection.
infographic.watch_item: Long-range ansatzes do not outperform short-range counterparts in every unsupervised regime, and the abstract provides no quantitative resource savings.
infographic.paper_title: Digital-Analog Quantum Neural Network with Long-Range Interactions

title: Generalized Mean-Field Ising Model as a Benchmark Family with Exact Solutions
authors: Madita Willsch, Gopal Chandra Santra, Dennis Willsch, Samuel Morales, Lukas Mauth, Vrinda Mehta
abstract: Exactly solvable models provide opportunities to understand complex optimization problems while offering controlled benchmarks for computational methods. However, nontrivial models that combine analytical tractability with challenging optimization structure remain scarce. Here, we introduce the Generalized Mean-Field Ising (GMFI) family, a densely connected and inhomogeneous class of Ising Hamiltonians whose ground states can nevertheless be obtained exactly. This exact solution reveals a hidden low-dimensional structure and enables a complete number-theoretic classification of different system sizes and degenerate ground states. Uniquely, the GMFI family can be used to benchmark both quantum and classical optimization methods over system sizes far beyond exact diagonalization. We investigate the GMFI family using several approaches, including theoretical analysis of quantum annealing, experiments on a D-Wave quantum processor, the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), imaginary-time evolution (ITE), greedy algorithm, simulated annealing, and a quantum-inspired greedy algorithm. Despite the GMFI model's exact solvability, it exhibits nontrivial algorithmic behavior: although the quantum-annealing gap is expected to decrease with increasing system size, it shows pronounced and unexpected system-size-dependent oscillatory signatures. These results establish GMFI models as a rare bridge between exact many-body theory, number theory, optimization, and quantum hardware, providing a scalable benchmark for identifying and understanding algorithmic limitations in classical and quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: The Generalized Mean-Field Ising (GMFI) family combines dense, inhomogeneous interactions with exact ground-state solutions, enabling scalable benchmarks for quantum and classical optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: GMFI offers exact reference solutions at sizes beyond exact diagonalization, helping engineers diagnose optimizer limitations without losing a known target.
method: Derive exact ground states through hidden low-dimensional structure.
Classify system sizes and ground-state degeneracies using number theory.
Evaluate quantum annealing, QAOA, imaginary-time evolution, and classical optimization methods.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical analysis, D-Wave experiments, and multiple optimizer evaluations, highlighting unexpected system-size-dependent oscillations in the quantum-annealing gap.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on this specially structured, exactly solvable family may not generalize to arbitrary Ising optimization problems.
infographic.paper_title: Generalized Mean-Field Ising Model as a Benchmark Family with Exact Solutions

title: A VLSI-Like Design and Verification Flow for Quantum Circuits: A Case Study in PI Estimation
authors: Yu-Ting Kao, Yeong-Jar Chang
abstract: This paper proposes a VLSI-like design and verification flow for quantum circuit implementation, covering four levels: behavioral modeling, register-transfer level (RTL), gate level, and full-circuit integration with quantum algorithms. Using quantum Monte Carlo methods for pi estimation as a case study, the proposed flow provides a systematic path from initial specifications to large-scale quantum circuit implementation. The paper highlights two key contributions. First, quantum digital design supports a broad range of applications beyond predefined circuit templates. This capability is particularly important for application-specific operations in algorithms such as Shor's, Grover's, and quantum amplitude estimation (QAE), and can significantly advance fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). Second, classical simulation shows that replacing random sampling with grid sampling can achieve a quadratic improvement in this pi-estimation case without quantum computation. This suggests that the quadratic speedup may arise from the grid sampling strategy rather than from the QAE circuit itself. By adapting conventional VLSI digital design principles, this four-level flow addresses a key bottleneck in quantum circuit design and enables flexible design initiation from multiple entry points, including specifications, RTL, and gate-level descriptions, paving the way for the practical deployment of quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: A four-level, VLSI-inspired workflow enables systematic quantum circuit design, while the pi-estimation case study suggests grid sampling—not QAE alone—may explain the observed quadratic improvement.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow supports application-specific quantum operations and design entry from specifications, RTL, or gates, offering a path toward scalable, fault-tolerant implementations.
method: Organize design and verification across behavioral, RTL, gate, and full-circuit integration levels.
Apply the workflow to quantum Monte Carlo pi estimation.
Compare random and grid sampling through classical simulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports classical simulations showing quadratic improvement from replacing random sampling with grid sampling in this pi-estimation case.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no hardware validation or resource estimates, and the sampling result should not be generalized to all QAE applications.
infographic.paper_title: A VLSI-Like Design and Verification Flow for Quantum Circuits: A Case Study in PI Estimation

title: Quantum Computing through Computational Imaging: Representations, Measurement, and Inference
authors: George Kourousias, Sergio Carrato, Roberto Pugliese, Panagiotis Dimitrakis, Alberto Carini
abstract: An algebraic correspondence between an imaging model and a quantum state does not specify a computational method: input access, measurement and decoding determine what can be returned. This exposition develops four distinctions for computational-imaging and engineering readers. It separates amplitude encodings of input values from encodings of complete candidate labelings, explaining why amplitude storage does not provide full-array readout. Complex-field interference motivates unknown-phase inference: complementary measurements resolve ambiguities that local Fisher information alone does not detect. Reshaping joint amplitudes into a matrix connects singular-value decomposition to pure-state entanglement, while distinguishing Schmidt rank from conditions for efficient classical simulation. In a four-pixel segmentation, an objective becomes a cost operator and a sampling circuit. One layer of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) lowers mean energy from $1.675$ to $0.686$ relative to uniform sampling, yet makes a nonoptimal labeling more probable than the optimum 0.484 versus 0.365. Archived IBM and IQM measurements illustrate a separate six-variable local boundary decision. Low-rank state reconstruction and selected quantum algorithms connect these distinctions to an end-to-end resource account. The derivations and reproducible numerical references assume complex linear algebra and probability, without prior quantum mechanics. The accompanying Seeing Amplitudes browser laboratory supports interactive exploration; the article remains self-contained and connects each representation to the estimate or decision it permits and the resources that output requires.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum representations become useful computational methods only when input access, measurement, and decoding support the desired estimate or decision.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Imaging engineers must evaluate end-to-end resources and output requirements rather than infer computational advantage from compact quantum encodings.
method: Distinguish amplitude encoding of input values from encoding complete candidate labelings.
Use complementary measurements for unknown-phase inference and matrix SVD to explain pure-state entanglement.
Translate a four-pixel segmentation objective into a cost operator and a QAOA sampling circuit.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the four-pixel example, one QAOA layer reduces mean energy from 1.675 to 0.686 versus uniform sampling, but a nonoptimal labeling is more probable than the optimum (0.484 versus 0.365); archived IBM and IQM measurements illustrate a separate six-variable boundary decision.
infographic.watch_item: Amplitude storage does not enable full-array readout, and lower mean energy does not guarantee that the optimal solution is sampled most often.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Computing through Computational Imaging: Representations, Measurement, and Inference

title: Provably efficient experimental classification of quantum data with quantum kernels
authors: Keitaro Anai, Akimoto Nakayama, Shintaro Ooka, Hiroko Tomoda, Yuto Morohoshi, Yohji Chin
abstract: Analyzing quantum systems is essential for quantum information processing, but can require exponentially many measurements without exploiting the structure of the system or task. Quantum machine learning offers a promising way to reduce this cost by learning from quantum data. Here, we theoretically establish a framework for efficient quantum-state classification and experimentally demonstrate the resulting scheme on a programmable photonic processor. Our analysis links learning efficiency to the structure of quantum data, without relying on a physical description tailored to each task. We derive sufficient conditions for accurate classification with a number of measurements polynomial in system size. We apply this guarantee to a resource problem in continuous-variable (CV) quantum computing: classifying stellar rank, a measure of non-Gaussianity. Experimentally, we implement the classification of single-mode CV quantum states with stellar rank zero and one. This is enabled by developing a programmable CV photonic processor capable of preparing and processing diverse Gaussian and non-Gaussian states and performing virtual projection onto such states, going beyond the Gaussian-only capabilities of most existing photonic platforms. The experiment demonstrates accurate classification despite experimental imperfections. Our results establish a theory-guided and experimentally validated framework for quantum-state classification that can be implemented on quantum devices available today.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum-kernel classification can require only polynomially many measurements when quantum data satisfy sufficient structural conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A programmable photonic processor demonstrates a route to classifying quantum resources without a task-specific physical model.
method: Derive sufficient conditions linking quantum-data structure to measurement-efficient classification.
Apply the framework to stellar rank, a measure of continuous-variable non-Gaussianity.
Prepare Gaussian and non-Gaussian states and perform virtual projections on a programmable photonic processor.
infographic.evidence_signal: The experiment accurately classified single-mode states with stellar rank zero versus one despite experimental imperfections; the abstract provides no numerical accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: The experimental demonstration is limited to single-mode, rank-zero versus rank-one states; broader scaling remains to be demonstrated.
infographic.paper_title: Provably efficient experimental classification of quantum data with quantum kernels

title: Force Sensing in a Recoverable Bosonic Quantum Memory
authors: Tairong Bai, Wen Zheng, Haoyang Cai, Xianke Li, Yangyang Ge, Kun Zhou
abstract: In continuous-variable quantum information, sensing and quantum error correction in the same mode face an intrinsic trade-off: sensors must accumulate weak external displacements, whereas bosonic codes typically suppress such shifts as errors. Here, we establish compatibility by constructing finite-energy bosonic codes that enable a single oscillator to sense an external force while actively protecting an unknown logical qubit. By encoding logical amplitudes across discrete wave-packet sites and capturing the force signal in a shared internal coordinate, we achieve an endpoint probe readout that is independent of the logical state under continuous photon loss $γ$. Crucially, binomial site recovery cancels packet-dependent probe distortions alongside logical errors: for a $(2r+2)$-packet code, memory infidelity is suppressed to $O(γ^{r+1})$ while residual memory-probe correlations scale as $O(γ^{r+2})$. Finally, superconducting quantum circuit benchmarks under competing photon-number dephasing and Kerr nonlinearity identify preferred encoding regimes for hardware implementation.

infographic.key_insight: Finite-energy bosonic codes let one oscillator sense an external force while protecting an unknown logical qubit, separating the force signal from logical information.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could combine force sensing and recoverable quantum memory in superconducting hardware without dedicating separate oscillator modes to each task.
method: Encode logical amplitudes across discrete wave-packet sites and store the force signal in a shared internal coordinate.
Read out the endpoint probe independently of the logical state under continuous photon loss.
Apply binomial site recovery to correct logical errors and packet-dependent probe distortions.
infographic.evidence_signal: For a (2r+2)-packet code, the abstract reports memory infidelity of O(γ^(r+1)) and residual memory–probe correlations of O(γ^(r+2)), plus superconducting-circuit benchmarks with photon-number dephasing and Kerr nonlinearity.
infographic.watch_item: Hardware performance depends on competing dephasing and Kerr effects; the abstract does not establish experimental realization.
infographic.paper_title: Force Sensing in a Recoverable Bosonic Quantum Memory

title: Grow, Compress, and Perturb: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Pathway to Scalable Quantum Chemistry on Quantum Computers
authors: Hugo D. Nogueira, Siwar Badreddine, Olivier Adjoua, Diata Traore, Guillaume Michel, Jean-Philip Piquemal
abstract: While Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) variants are among leading candidates for electronic structure calculations on quantum computers, gradient-based operator selection limits their scalability. To solve this, we introduce the Hamiltonian-gradient-free VULCAN (Variational Upbuilding, Layered Compression, Adaptive N-body perturbation) layered VQE framework. Our method dynamically generates ansatz operators using Variational Double Bracket Flow (VDBF) equations. Combined with a linearly scaling minimal complete pool, it creates a pool 4-12 times smaller than QEB (Qubit-Excitation-Based) pools. By appending entire layers simultaneously, Hamiltonian gradient measurements are completely eliminated. Circuit depth is managed via a grow-then-compress scheme using efficient state-overlap measurements, and qubit requirements are reduced by projecting the Hamiltonian onto a dominant-determinant subspace. Using high-performance emulation up to 32 logical qubits, we achieve chemical accuracy at just 5-20% of the measurement cost of batched ADAPT-VQE for hydrogen chains, BeH2 and H2O. For the 32-qubit C3H6, where batched ADAPT-VQE does not reach chemical accuracy, a single VULCAN layer combined with a GPU-accelerated stochastic Epstein-Nesbet (ENPT2) correction does. This stochastic ENPT2 post-processing step enables early termination at chemical accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: VULCAN combines Hamiltonian-gradient-free ansatz growth, circuit compression, and perturbative correction to reduce the measurement cost of quantum chemistry calculations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets measurement overhead, circuit depth, and qubit requirements, offering a resource-efficient pathway toward larger quantum chemistry simulations.
method: Grow full operator layers using Variational Double Bracket Flow and a linearly scaling pool, avoiding Hamiltonian-gradient measurements for operator selection.
Compress circuits through state-overlap measurements and reduce qubit requirements via dominant-determinant subspace projection.
Apply GPU-accelerated stochastic Epstein–Nesbet perturbation theory (ENPT2) to recover residual correlation and enable early termination.
infographic.evidence_signal: Emulation up to 32 logical qubits reports chemical accuracy at 5–20% of batched ADAPT-VQE's measurement cost for hydrogen chains, BeH2, and H2O; one VULCAN layer plus ENPT2 also reaches chemical accuracy for 32-qubit C3H6.
infographic.watch_item: Results rely on emulation; robustness to hardware noise and the total cost of compression and classical ENPT2 post-processing remain implementation concerns.
infographic.paper_title: Grow, Compress, and Perturb: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Pathway to Scalable Quantum Chemistry on Quantum Computers

title: Strict Frequency Bandwidths from Causal Light Cones Enable Scalable Exact Gradient Evaluation in Quantum Optimization
authors: Zhaoyang Song, Wei Zhang, Ji Cao, Xuexi Yi, Hong-Fu Wang
abstract: Dynamical locality is often regarded as a limitation of shallow quantum circuits, yet we show that it can reduce the number of circuit settings required for exact evaluation of gradients with respect to shared parameters. For layered ansatze generated by commuting local terms, strict Heisenberg light cones confine energy slices obtained by varying one shared layer parameter to finite Fourier bandwidths dictated by local causal geometry. This bandlimit recasts exact gradient evaluation as a local signal recovery problem and, when the relevant frequencies lie on a known frequency lattice, yields an exact multipoint parameter-shift rule based on the discrete sine transform. The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) provides a canonical realization in which this mechanism is governed by the local structure of the graph. Specifically, when a cost angle is varied, the relevant geometry is encoded by the contact region in the interaction line graph. At fixed circuit depth on graphs of bounded degree, the number of distinct circuit settings required for the corresponding derivative collapses from $O(m)$ to $O(1)$. This shows that dynamical locality is not merely a constraint on correlation propagation, but also a computational resource that enables exact gradient evaluation with fewer circuit settings in quantum optimization.

infographic.key_insight: Strict causal light cones bound the Fourier bandwidth of shared-parameter energy slices, enabling exact quantum-circuit gradients from fewer circuit settings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For QAOA at fixed depth on bounded-degree graphs, the number of distinct circuit settings for a cost-angle derivative drops from O(m) to O(1), where m is the number of cost terms.
method: Use Heisenberg light cones to bound energy-slice frequencies in layered ansatze generated by commuting local terms.
Recover exact derivatives with a discrete-sine-transform multipoint parameter-shift rule when frequencies lie on a known lattice.
For QAOA cost angles, determine the relevant bandwidth from contact regions in the interaction line graph.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical bandwidth result and circuit-setting scaling reduction, but provides no numerical benchmarks or hardware evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: The O(1) setting count assumes fixed depth and bounded graph degree; exact recovery also requires a known frequency lattice and does not eliminate finite-shot estimation noise.
infographic.paper_title: Strict Frequency Bandwidths from Causal Light Cones Enable Scalable Exact Gradient Evaluation in Quantum Optimization

title: Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins
authors: El Mustapha Mansouri, Eikichi Kimura, Masato Koga, Keigo Arai
abstract: An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another's work and can stop or redirect investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical checks and conduct experiments designed to challenge their claims. We demonstrate these capabilities by investigating ensembles of quantum spins in diamond. The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally.

infographic.key_insight: Collaborating AI agents derived and experimentally tested a minimum-calibration result for quantum spins in diamond, rejecting an initially promising but drift-affected experiment as inconclusive.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Agent-based cross-checks and reference measurements offer a route to more reliable autonomous characterization of quantum hardware.
method: Generate and critique research questions, with authority to stop or redirect investigations.
Derive minimum calibration requirements for a defined family of microwave pulse sequences and check them computationally.
Design discriminating experiments and revise measurement protocols when reference measurements reveal drift.
infographic.evidence_signal: The initial experiment was deemed inconclusive because of signal drift; a revised experiment met unchanged acceptance criteria and supported the theoretical predictions.
infographic.watch_item: The demonstration concerns a defined pulse-sequence family and diamond spin ensembles; broader hardware applicability and quantitative performance are not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins

title: Execution bias, repeatability and mitigation cost in parameter-frozen molecular VQE energy evaluation
authors: Julen Larrucea
abstract: A smaller statistical error bar need not mean a more accurate molecular energy. We evaluate noiselessly optimized molecular variational quantum eigensolver states on IBM Aachen and Pittsburgh, two 156-qubit Heron processors (provider-reported revision 3). Only energy evaluation runs on hardware, with parameters, layouts and compiled circuits frozen and dynamical decoupling disabled. A five-molecule pilot, three-molecule isolated cohort in three windows and known-state controls comprise 110 jobs and 28.2 billed quantum processing unit (QPU) minutes; the isolated cohort spans 30.2 h within a 31.7 h campaign. Raw 1024 O2 and BeH2 mean residuals exceed returned uncertainty by factors 12-32. Pittsburgh BeH2 cross-job standard deviation is 5.6 times mean returned uncertainty. The zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) package reduces O2 absolute residuals by 49.7% on Aachen and 83.5% on Pittsburgh at about fourfold charge. On Pittsburgh, twirled readout error extinction (TREX) removes 80 millihartree (mHa) per Raw 1024 job charge versus 50 mHa for ZNE. Controls reveal qubit-124 preparation or readout errors 5.4-5.6 times calibration; 13 mitigated energy point estimates fall outside the mapped spectrum, with no Raw counterpart. These results support workload checks and repeated measurements before additional sampling.

infographic.key_insight: Smaller reported uncertainty did not guarantee accurate molecular VQE energies: hardware execution bias and cross-job variability could dominate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Validate workload-specific bias and repeatability before buying more shots or mitigation, since mitigation gains can carry substantial QPU cost.
method: Evaluate noiselessly optimized molecular VQE states on IBM Aachen and Pittsburgh 156-qubit Heron processors.
Freeze parameters, layouts and compiled circuits, with dynamical decoupling disabled.
Compare raw and mitigated energies across molecular cohorts, repeated windows and known-state controls.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 110 jobs and 28.2 billed QPU minutes, Raw 1024 O2 and BeH2 mean residuals were 12–32 times returned uncertainty; ZNE reduced O2 absolute residuals by 49.7–83.5% at about fourfold charge.
infographic.watch_item: Mitigated estimates require physical-validity checks: 13 energy point estimates fell outside the mapped spectrum, versus none for raw estimates.
infographic.paper_title: Execution bias, repeatability and mitigation cost in parameter-frozen molecular VQE energy evaluation

title: Toric codes all the way down: decoupling translation-invariant topological CSS codes in higher dimensions
authors: Mingxin He, Yifei Wang, Hao Song, Yingfei Gu
abstract: Topological Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes in more than two spatial dimensions offer features useful for fault-tolerant quantum computation, such as transversal non-Clifford gates and single-shot decoding, but a systematic understanding of them is still lacking. One approach is to decouple a code: map it to a stack of higher-form toric codes by a finite-depth local CSS-preserving Clifford circuit, possibly after adding ancillas. For translation-invariant $p$-ary CSS codes, where $p$ is prime ($p=2$ for qubits), we require the circuit to commute with the translations of a superlattice. In two dimensions, such a decoupling exists once these translations act trivially on every anyon type. In higher dimensions, excitations are sorted by their dimension into superselection layers, which can remain glued together even when translations act trivially on each layer. We show that this gluing is the only remaining obstruction: a code can be decoupled on a superlattice exactly when, after coarse-graining to it, translations act trivially on every layer and the gluing vanishes. Moreover, for a code with finitely many excitation types in each layer and $m$ nonzero layers, once translations act trivially on every layer, further coarse-graining by a factor of $p^{m-1}$ in every direction removes the aforementioned gluing. Physically, the same criterion determines when the code encodes the maximal number of logical qudits on a finite torus. Finally, we give an explicit algorithm that constructs the decoupling as a circuit of SUM (qudit CNOT) and SWAP gates.

infographic.key_insight: Translation-invariant topological CSS codes decouple into stacks of higher-form toric codes exactly when superlattice translations act trivially on every excitation layer and interlayer gluing vanishes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This criterion and an explicit circuit-construction algorithm provide a systematic way to simplify higher-dimensional quantum error-correcting codes for fault-tolerant computing.
method: Organize excitations into dimensional superselection layers and identify translation action and interlayer gluing.
For prime-p qudits with m nonzero layers and finitely many excitation types per layer, remove gluing by further coarse-graining by p^(m−1) in every direction once translations act trivially.
Construct a finite-depth, local, CSS-preserving Clifford decoupling circuit using SUM and SWAP gates, possibly with ancillas.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an exact decoupling theorem, a coarse-graining bound, and a constructive algorithm, but no numerical benchmarks or hardware evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: The coarse-graining factor can grow rapidly with the number of excitation layers, and practical circuit and ancilla overheads are not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Toric codes all the way down: decoupling translation-invariant topological CSS codes in higher dimensions

title: Algebraic strong-to-weak symmetry breaking and partial decodability in the surface code
authors: Stephen W. Yan, Yimu Bao, Sagar Vijay
abstract: Coherent noise can give rise to unconventional regimes of quantum information recovery and mixed-state order. We study these phenomena in two settings related by Wegner duality: the triangular-lattice surface code subject to single-qubit Pauli-$Z$ rotations followed by syndrome measurements, and a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ paramagnet subject to strongly symmetric decoherence. Increasing the rotation angle drives a transition from a decodable phase to a \emph{partially decodable} critical phase in the code, and from a strongly symmetric phase to a phase with \emph{algebraic} $\mathbb{Z}_2$ strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SWSSB) in the dual paramagnet. We develop a common description of these phenomena in terms of a weakly coupled $\mathrm{SO}(n)$ nonlinear sigma model in the replica limit $n\to1$. Taking this replica limit analytically, we derive universal signatures of the critical phase: an optimal Pauli decoding fidelity that approaches a universal function of the system's aspect ratio in the thermodynamic limit, and a dual fidelity correlator that decays as a universal power law. These observables relate to correlations of twist operators in the sigma model description. Large-scale numerical simulations confirm these analytical predictions. We also argue that the algebraic SWSSB phase cannot be realized by any Pauli dephasing channel acting on the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ paramagnet. We probe this "non-classical" character through the output state's sensitivity to well-separated $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ fluxes inserted in the initial state, which reveals persistent coherence between distinct $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ charge trajectories at long distances.

infographic.key_insight: Coherent noise drives the triangular-lattice surface code into a partially decodable critical phase, dual to algebraic strong-to-weak symmetry breaking in a quantum paramagnet.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results show that coherent errors can produce recovery regimes beyond a simple decodable-versus-undecodable picture, motivating noise-aware evaluation of surface-code decoders.
method: Study single-qubit Pauli-Z rotations followed by syndrome measurements in the surface code.
Relate decoding to strongly symmetric decoherence in a dual Z₂ paramagnet.
Derive universal observables using an SO(n) nonlinear sigma model in the replica limit n→1.
infographic.evidence_signal: Large-scale numerical simulations confirm analytical predictions for aspect-ratio-dependent optimal Pauli decoding fidelity and power-law decay of the dual fidelity correlator.
infographic.watch_item: The predictions concern a specific coherent-noise model and optimal Pauli decoding; practical decoder performance under realistic mixed noise remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Algebraic strong-to-weak symmetry breaking and partial decodability in the surface code

title: Fault-Tolerant Heisenberg-Limited Quantum Metrology with Bosonic Probes
authors: Daniel G. Li, Lorcán O Conlon, Yu-Xin Wang, Erfan Abbasgholinejad, Twesh Upadhyaya, Alexey V. Gorshkov
abstract: Quantum sensors have been shown to enable more precise measurements than classical sensors. By using entanglement and coherent evolution, the estimation error can be made to scale better in interrogation time, photon count, and other resources, achieving Heisenberg-limited scaling. However, environmental noise and hardware errors typically destroy the coherence of the sensitive quantum states. This motivates the use of fault-tolerant techniques to create more robust quantum sensing protocols. Such fault-tolerant quantum sensing approaches have been shown to enhance sensitivity for qubit systems, but many practical sensors require bosonic probes. In this paper, we propose a fault-tolerant protocol using bosons to estimate displacements in the presence of dephasing noise. We construct an optimal error-correcting code under a mean photon-number constraint. Controlled displacements couple the probe to a repetition-encoded qubit register, while repeated boson-parity measurements and resets remove probe noise without erasing the stored logical phase. Under circuit-level bit-flip noise, a distance-$d$ code suppresses logical failures to order $p^{(d+1)/2}$. We show that, for a decay rate $γ_A$, a total sensing time $T$ and a mean photon number budget $N$, and for sufficiently small residual signals, the Fisher information scales as $NT^2$ over interrogation times of order $γ_A^{-(d+1)/2}$. This is a significant improvement over the non-fault-tolerant approach that achieves Heisenberg scaling only for a total time $\mathcal O(γ_A^{-1})$.

infographic.key_insight: A fault-tolerant bosonic sensing protocol preserves Heisenberg-limited time scaling under dephasing by storing the signal phase in an error-corrected qubit register.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The protocol could extend precision-sensing durations beyond the probe’s noise-limited timescale using controlled displacements, parity measurements, and resets.
method: Construct an optimal bosonic error-correcting code under a mean photon-number constraint.
Couple the probe to a repetition-encoded qubit register through controlled displacements.
Repeatedly measure boson parity and reset the probe to remove noise while preserving the stored logical phase.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical scaling: distance-d encoding suppresses logical failures to order p^((d+1)/2), with Fisher information scaling as NT² over sensing times of order γ_A^(-(d+1)/2).
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees require sufficiently small residual signals and a circuit-level bit-flip noise model; experimental robustness to broader hardware errors is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Fault-Tolerant Heisenberg-Limited Quantum Metrology with Bosonic Probes

title: Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization for Variable Molecular Geometries
authors: Matthieu Fortin-Deschenes, Ibrahim Shehzad
abstract: Quantum and hybrid quantum-classical algorithms have the potential to improve the accuracy and scale of quantum chemistry and impact a broad range of applications such as drug discovery and catalysis. In particular, subspace methods such as sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) can already tackle classically challenging systems. However, practical algorithms that go beyond the computation of electronic ground and excited states are still scarce. Here, we introduce the variable-geometry sample-based quantum diagonalization (VGSQD) algorithm, which extends SQD to variable molecular geometries by reusing quantum samples from a reference geometry at displaced ones, thus significantly reducing quantum computational cost. Using circuits of up to 124 qubits on ibm-quebec, an IBM Heron r2 quantum processor, we determine the equilibrium geometry and energy of the weakly bound, strongly correlated beryllium dimer, as well as the water molecule. Finally, we extend VGSQD to chemical reactions and compute the minimum energy path and energy barrier of a hydrogen exchange reaction. The results are comparable with state-of-the-art classical methods such as CCSD(T) and DMRG. This work broadens the scope of quantum algorithms for chemistry, from energies to geometry optimization and reaction pathways, both essential for practical applications.

infographic.key_insight: Variable-geometry sample-based quantum diagonalization (VGSQD) reuses quantum samples across molecular geometries, extending quantum chemistry calculations to geometry optimization and reaction pathways with reduced quantum computational cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reusing samples could make hybrid quantum-classical workflows more practical for molecular structure and reaction studies relevant to catalysis and drug discovery.
method: Generate quantum samples at a reference molecular geometry.
Reuse those samples for SQD calculations at displaced geometries.
Use the resulting energies to optimize structures and trace reaction pathways.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using circuits of up to 124 qubits on IBM's ibm-quebec Heron r2 processor, the authors studied beryllium dimer and water equilibrium properties and a hydrogen exchange reaction pathway, reporting results comparable to CCSD(T) and DMRG.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify computational savings or establish how reliably reference-geometry samples transfer across larger structural changes.
infographic.paper_title: Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization for Variable Molecular Geometries

title: Quantum-Walk Inspired Spectral Metrics for Evaluating QAOA Mixers
authors: Jasjyot Singh Gulati, Tharrmashastha SAPV
abstract: QAOA mixers play an important role in enabling exploration of the exponentially large solution space of binary optimization problems. However, the choice of mixer Hamiltonian is typically guided by convention and implementation or circuit constraints, rather than by a graph-topology-aware criterion. In this work, inspired by quantum-walk mixing theory, we propose two complementary spectral heuristics for characterizing QAOA mixer topologies. The first is the normalized minimum eigenvalue separation of the mixer Hamiltonian $H_M$, while the second is the long-time averaged minimum eigenvalue separation of the mixer unitary $U_M(β)=e^{-iβH_M}$. Both quantities are invariant under any positive rescaling of the mixer Hamiltonian and provide Hamiltonian- and unitary-level characterizations of the mixer's spectral structure. We use them as heuristic indicators of the mixer dynamics relevant to amplitude redistribution during QAOA evolution. We derive exact expressions and asymptotic bounds for the complete graph, hypercube, cycle, and balanced 2-D torus, revealing a broad spectral separation between the studied topology classes. We then compare these separations with empirical QAOA performance. For random permutation-invariant cost Hamiltonians, the observed performance ordering is broadly consistent with the spectral characterization. In contrast, for structured 1-D and 2-D Ising QUBOs, this ordering breaks down, indicating that mixer-cost alignment can become important. These results illustrate both the usefulness and the limitations of topology-level, cost-agnostic spectral heuristics for QAOA mixer selection.

infographic.key_insight: Two scale-invariant spectral heuristics help characterize QAOA mixer topologies, but their agreement with performance depends on the cost structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These metrics offer topology-aware guidance for mixer selection beyond convention and circuit constraints, while highlighting the need to assess mixer–cost alignment.
method: Measure normalized minimum eigenvalue separation of the mixer Hamiltonian.
Measure long-time averaged minimum eigenvalue separation of the mixer unitary.
Derive exact expressions and asymptotic bounds for complete graphs, hypercubes, cycles, and balanced 2-D tori.
infographic.evidence_signal: Empirical QAOA performance broadly follows the spectral characterization for random permutation-invariant costs, but not for structured 1-D and 2-D Ising QUBOs.
infographic.watch_item: These cost-agnostic heuristics do not guarantee QAOA performance; structured problems can require mixer–cost alignment.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum-Walk Inspired Spectral Metrics for Evaluating QAOA Mixers

title: Structural Bottlenecks in QAOA Mixer Design: Transport and Causal Reach
authors: Jasjyot Singh Gulati, Tharrmashastha SAPV
abstract: The choice of mixer is a central design decision in the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), yet different structural limitations of a mixer need not be captured by a single metric. We identify two complementary structural bottlenecks for shallow QAOA: configuration-space transport, which limits how strongly probability can concentrate on high-quality solutions, and finite-depth causal reach, which limits which parts of a problem instance can influence a local objective term. In Part I, we derive first-order mixer-dependent objective bounds in complementary small-$β$ and small-$γ$ regimes. For connected regular mixer graphs, the two leading-order expressions are exactly equivalent through a graph-Laplacian identity and reduce to the same cost-weighted Dirichlet energy. We then derive a non-perturbative upper envelope from the layer-wise $\ell_1$ spreading of the mixer unitary, yielding a cost-distribution-dependent necessary spreading condition for attaining a target approximation ratio. In Part II, we study the locality bottleneck for MaxCut by augmenting the transverse-field mixer with problem-graph-aligned two-local interactions. The resulting $k$-hop construction has causal radius at most $(k+1)p$ at depth $p$; for the $k=1$ architectures studied numerically, this gives radius $2p$. Across cycles, circular ladders, and high-girth regular bipartite graphs, $X{+}XX$ and $X{+}YY$ improve the best-found approximation ratios over the standard $X$ mixer at equal depth, while $X{+}YY$ at depth $p$ comes within about one approximation-ratio point of plain $X$ at depth $2p$ in the reach-matched cases examined. The unequal performance of the equal-reach $XX$ and $YY$ augmentations shows that satisfying a structural capability does not by itself guarantee performance. Together, the results provide complementary structural insights for mixer design.

infographic.key_insight: QAOA mixer design faces two complementary bottlenecks: probability transport across configurations and finite-depth causal reach across the problem graph.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Problem-aligned two-local mixers can improve shallow-circuit approximation ratios, but greater causal reach alone does not guarantee better performance.
method: Derive small-angle objective bounds linked by a graph-Laplacian identity.
Bound achievable concentration using layer-wise mixer-unitary spreading.
Evaluate X+XX and X+YY mixers for MaxCut, with causal radius at most 2p at depth p.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across cycles, circular ladders, and high-girth regular bipartite graphs, augmented mixers improved best-found ratios at equal depth; X+YY at depth p came within about one approximation-ratio point of X at depth 2p in examined reach-matched cases.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern best-found numerical performance on selected graph families, not guaranteed gains or hardware-level resource savings.
infographic.paper_title: Structural Bottlenecks in QAOA Mixer Design: Transport and Causal Reach

title: Dynamical quantum simulations as laboratories for quantum information
authors: Su Yeon Chang, Hailey S. Murray, Brian Barch, Greeshma Oruganti, Luis Pedro García-Pintos, Martin Larocca
abstract: Dynamical quantum simulations are commonly designed to access a particular response function or correlation function. Yet the underlying protocol prepares a family of many-body states that contains information well beyond the observable for which the simulation was originally designed. In this work, we explore the idea of using these states as laboratories for quantum information. As a case study, we consider the local-pulse protocols used to compute Green functions in finite XX and XXX spin chains, and we interpret opposite source rotations as encoding a classical bit into the many-body system. This allows us to follow how the resulting record propagates, how it is encoded across local subsystems, and how readily it can be accessed with different measurements. We also find a clear separation between representation and readout. While fermionic covariance data exactly reconstruct the signed response in the XX chain, simple spin measurements recover a larger fraction of the locally available information in the XXX chain. This reversed ordering persists when we move from finite-pulse discrimination to local source-angle estimation. Going beyond the source record, the same reduced states also allow us to reinterpret results in terms of Bell state recovery and quantum communication rates, as well as providing direct access to the evolving bipartite and genuine multipartite entanglement of the system. Our results show that dynamical quantum simulations developed for response calculations can naturally be used to ask a much broader set of quantum-information questions about the many-body states they already prepare.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum simulations designed to calculate response functions also prepare many-body states that reveal how information propagates, becomes locally accessible, and supports entanglement-based tasks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Existing response-simulation protocols could support additional quantum-information analyses without redesigning state preparation, though measurement and analysis requirements may differ.
method: Study local-pulse Green-function protocols in finite XX and XXX spin chains.
Encode a classical bit using opposite source rotations and track its propagation and accessibility in local subsystems.
Compare covariance-based reconstruction and spin-measurement readout, then analyze source-angle estimation, Bell-state recovery, communication rates, and entanglement.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the studied chains, fermionic covariance data exactly reconstruct the signed XX response, yet simple spin measurements recover a larger fraction of locally available information in XXX; this ordering persists for local source-angle estimation.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern finite spin-chain case studies; scalability and robustness to experimental noise are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamical quantum simulations as laboratories for quantum information
